title: What is Good Professional Development?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. sets out a list of considerations for designing professional development that respects teachers as professionals. He starts from the observation that poor PD is part of why teachers leave a profession that does not always feel professional. Good PD, he says, is efficient and minimalistic, humane, coherent, free of buzzwords and respectful of every department in the room. It should aim at longevity, favoring ideas that can last years, and remind teachers why the work is worthwhile. He also asks for treating teachers as clear thinkers rather than technicians, building collective efficacy, leaving time for reflective application, and having credible facilitators.
points: Efficiency matters because teachers' top complaint is lack of time, so PD should offer minimalistic strategies and not fill time.
PD should be humane and coherent, giving memorable frameworks instead of a pile of random strategies.
Plan around longevity: the shorter an idea's shelf life, the shorter the PD, and always remind teachers why the job is good.
Treat teachers as professionals through divergent-view reading, classroom video clips and shared efficacy rather than technician training.
Protect time for reflective application, since skipping it to save time means the learning does not stick.
quotes: One reason teachers leave the profession is surely that the profession doesn’t feel all that professional sometimes. This is caused, in part, by poor professional development.
The PD facilitator aims to achieve something in the shortest amount of time it takes. The shortest path is best because our time is limited.

What we’re building in our schools are centers for the promotion of long-term flourishing — not factories pumping out test scores. One way to do this is to make PD a time for connecting and laughing, too.
Most teachers need a dozen new and random strategies about as much as they need a lobotomy. This is why it’s so helpful to offer memorable frameworks within professional development.
The shorter the shelf life of an idea covered in a professional development, the shorter the PD ought to be — if the PD ought to be at all.
Good teachers are not the same as good technicians. The kinds of people we want at the heads of our classrooms are clear thinkers who learn constantly — not automaton technocrats.

Teachers need time to take what they’ve learned and integrate it into what they are already doing. Good PD includes time for this. When we skip this part to save time, we end up losing time because the professional development is so much less likely to stick.
